tldr: By running a massive vision–language model (VLM) only once at the start of an episode and having a lightweight online actor reference the resulting task memory, this approach keeps highly accurate closed-loop control while speeding up inference by up to over 17x.
hero_caption: Overview of Fast-VLA's performance and architecture. (a) shows a dramatic reduction in inference time and memory usage compared to other methods while maintaining high success rates. (b) illustrates the two-stage mechanism: a frozen VLM generates task memory once at the start of an episode, and a lightweight online actor then predicts actions based on current observations.
overview:
Vision–language–action (VLA) models powered by large pretrained vision–language models (VLMs) have attracted huge attention in robot manipulation. However, most conventional methods rerun the multi-billion-parameter VLM every few robot steps (for every action chunk). When humans perform a task, once they understand the overall goal, they simply move their hands quickly using visual and tactile feedback. They don't re-evaluate the meaning of the entire task from scratch at every single moment. This paper focuses on this difference in timescales between "task understanding" and "real-time control."

Guided by the idea "You Only Think Once," the authors propose Fast-VLA. At the start of an episode, the instruction and initial camera views are fed into a frozen 4B (4-billion-parameter) VLM. All 34 layers of its Key–Value (KV) cache are saved as a fixed "task memory." After that, the massive VLM leaves the control loop completely, leaving only a lightweight online actor to run during execution. The online actor constructs action queries from current camera views and joint states, retrieves the needed context from the fixed task memory, and predicts action chunks in a single pass.

Evaluated on the dual-arm RoboTwin 2.0 and single-arm LIBERO benchmarks, it achieved success rates on par with or better than existing VLA models (around 92.4% on RoboTwin 2.0). Furthermore, comparisons on the same hardware showed a 10.9–17.1x speedup in per-step amortized inference time, while keeping online resident memory down to just 1.22 GiB.
contributions: Proposed an episode-level VLA architecture that decouples task understanding from real-time control, restricting frozen 4B VLM inference to a single run at the start of each episode.

Developed a lightweight online actor that fuses current visual and proprioceptive feedback with learned queries to retrieve context from multi-layer fixed task memory and predict actions in a single pass.

Demonstrated on RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus that Fast-VLA speeds up inference time by 10.9–17.1x compared to prior methods and cuts memory usage down to 1.22 GiB while maintaining high success rates.

sections.heading: Pushing Massive VLMs Out of the Control Loop: "Think Once" with Fast-VLA
sections.summary: Conventional VLA models run a massive VLM every time they predict actions, creating a heavy computational burden. Inspired by how humans grasp the goal once before acting and then move quickly relying only on sensory feedback, Fast-VLA confines task understanding strictly to the initial step.
sections.details:
VLA models that integrate large pretrained VLMs into robot control offer a powerful framework capable of adapting flexibly to diverse instructions and environments. However, most existing models rerun multi-billion-parameter backbones at every control cycle. While a robot must observe its environment and fine-tune its movements in real time, the given task instructions and high-level goals barely change throughout an episode. This led to the fundamental question: "Do we really need to rethink the task from scratch with a massive VLM at every single step?"

When humans manipulate objects, they first figure out what needs to be done, identify the target object, and then reach out. While moving their hands, they adjust motions based on visual and tactile feedback, but they never re-interpret the high-level task meaning with every finger twitch. In other words, there are two distinct timescales: high-level "task understanding" is low-frequency and stable, whereas "low-level control" is high-frequency and responds to environmental changes.

To address this, the authors developed Fast-VLA, which "thinks once" at the beginning of an episode. Initial images and instructions are passed into a frozen 4B VLM, and the Key–Value tensors across all Transformer layers are stored as fixed "task memory." The VLM is then entirely removed from the control loop. During execution, a lightweight online actor receives current camera views and joint positions (proprioception), dynamically generates queries, and looks up the fixed task memory. This achieves massive inference speedups and memory savings while keeping the responsiveness needed for closed-loop control.

sections.heading: How Fast-VLA Differs from Prior Computational Efficiency Methods
sections.summary: Prior acceleration approaches mainly focused on parallel action generation or partial recomputation via caching. Fast-VLA takes a fundamentally different path by targeting the backbone invocation frequency itself, removing the VLM from the control loop entirely.
sections.details:
### Efficient VLA Policies
General VLA models combine the expressive power of VLMs with action generation mechanisms like autoregressive tokens, flow matching, or dedicated action heads. Recent research has attempted to reduce computation through parallel decoding of continuous actions, action chunking (predicting multi-step actions at once), and compact action tokenization. However, these are optimizations on the action generation side; they still run the massive VLM backbone whenever new observations arrive. In contrast, Fast-VLA fundamentally differs by reducing the backbone invocation frequency itself to once per episode. Unlike approaches like HyperVLA, which dynamically generate small policy weights from instructions and initial images, Fast-VLA uses shared weights for the online actor and retains task context as an explicit multi-layer KV memory.

### Computation Reuse Across Control Steps
Methods like VLA-Cache reuse token representations that change little between adjacent frames, and world-model approaches like WAM bypass video generation to save compute. However, these methods still keep massive visual models or video backbones inside the per-step control loop. Fast-VLA offloads all state estimation and visual feedback processing to a lightweight online actor, banishing the massive model entirely from the loop.

sections.heading: How Fixed Task Memory and the Lightweight Online Actor Work Together
sections.summary: A frozen 4B VLM creates 34 layers of KV task memory from initial views and instructions. During execution, a DINOv2-based lightweight actor creates action queries from current camera views and robot states, cross-attends with the fixed memory, and predicts action chunks in a single pass.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Overview
Fast-VLA is clearly divided into two stages: "Task Memory Construction" and "Online Actor Control." At the start of an episode, a fixed task memory $M$ is generated from language instruction $L$ and initial multi-camera images $I_0$. In the subsequent control loop, online input representations $Z_t$ are extracted from current observation images $I_t$, joint states (proprioception) $q_t$, and a short image history $H_t$. These are combined with the fixed task memory $M$ to predict an action chunk extending $K$ steps into the future in a single pass.

### 3.2 Episode-Level Task Memory
To generate task memory, Fast-VLA uses a frozen DM0.5 (a 4B-parameter VLM). Crucially, instead of keeping only the Transformer's final layer, it retains Key and Value tensors across all 34 layers. This allows the downstream actor to flexibly retrieve information at whatever depth it needs, from low-level visual features in shallow layers to high-level semantic context in deeper layers.

### 3.3 Online Actor
The online actor, which runs at every step during execution, consists of the following modules:
- **Live Inputs and Vision Encoders**: Processes head camera images, left/right wrist camera images, and short past frames. Each camera uses an independent, fine-tunable DINOv2 encoder.
- **Query Fusion**: Employs learnable queries indexed by future time steps $\tau$ and arms $a$. It fuses each arm's 7-dimensional joint state with the wrist camera's CLS token (global image feature) through an MLP via gated residual connections. This enables the actor to formulate distinct "action queries" tailored to current arm positions and local conditions, even when querying the exact same fixed task memory.
- **Action Decoder**: A 4-layer decoder structure where each layer processes Self-Attention (coordinating time and both arms), Cross-Visual (reading current visual tokens), Cross-Memory (retrieving from fixed task memory), and an FFN, in that order. The Cross-Memory stage introduces an adapter that weights and integrates KV memory across VLM layers using learnable scores for each decoder layer. Finally, a linear action head outputs 50 steps of joint targets ($50 \times 14$ dimensions) in a single forward pass without iterative sampling like diffusion models.

### 3.4 Training and Inference
Because the VLM backbone is fully frozen, KV caches for the task memory across training datasets can be precomputed and saved offline. As a result, only the actor's DINOv2 encoders and decoder need to be trained efficiently using an $\ell_1$ loss on normalized actions.

captions.F2: Overall architecture of Fast-VLA. In the upper stage, a frozen DM0.5 VLM generates 34 layers of KV task memory once from initial views and instructions. In the lower stage, the online actor fuses arm states and wrist camera features into learned queries, references current visual tokens and fixed task memory, and outputs a 50-step action chunk.

sections.heading: A 17x Speedup with High Manipulation Performance: Verified Across Diverse Benchmarks
sections.summary: Evaluations were conducted on RoboTwin 2.0 and LIBERO benchmarks. Fast-VLA maintained high success rates above 92% while achieving a 10.9–17.1x speedup over comparably performing baselines, confirming both the efficacy of fixed memory and dynamic attention shifts.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Performance and Inference Cost on RoboTwin 2.0
Fast-VLA was evaluated on the dual-arm RoboTwin 2.0 benchmark across both Clean environments and Randomized environments with varied backgrounds and objects. It achieved impressive success rates of 92.46% on Clean and 92.40% on Randomized (92.43% average). In benchmark comparisons on the same hardware, it sped up per-step amortized inference time (including initial VLM prefill) by 10.9–17.1x compared to existing baselines with over 90% success rates. For example, compared to DM0.5, Fast-VLA is 11.2x faster with only a 1.02-point difference in success rate; against Faster-WAM (HUST), it is 10.9x faster with just a 0.09-point difference. Additionally, online resident memory is kept to just 1.22 GiB (with the fixed task memory itself taking only 174.6 MiB).

### 4.2 Evaluations on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus
Fast-VLA was also evaluated on the single-arm LIBERO suite. It scored 95.95% on standard LIBERO and 79.11% on LIBERO-Plus, which introduces perturbations to test robustness. Compared to Faster-WAM (HUST), it was 5.54 points higher on LIBERO-Plus while running 21.2x faster.

### 4.3 Qualitative Observations and Visual Grounding
Even without updating task memory, the robot handles mid-task state transitions effectively. Attention visualizations during a block-stacking task revealed that when control shifted from the left arm to the right arm, head camera attention autonomously shifted from the red block to the green block. Even with fixed memory, changing wrist observations guide visual attention appropriately toward the currently active subgoal.

### 4.4 Ablation Studies and Analysis
- **Reliance on Task Memory**: In experiments swapping task memory with another episode at test time, swapping with a different episode of the same task caused the success rate to plummet to 6.26%. This proves that the actor relies precisely on memory tailored to initial conditions.
- **Memory Composition**: Completely removing task memory dropped success to 69.90% (on standard LIBERO), while using memory from all layers produced the highest performance.
- **Impact of Observations**: Removing wrist cameras caused success rates to plunge to 65.60%, demonstrating that local close-up views are vital for closed-loop control.
- **Update Frequency**: Updating memory every chunk improved success by only 1.8 points while worsening inference time by 3.12x, confirming that "once at episode start" offers the best trade-off.
- **Long-Horizon Tasks**: Even on tasks lasting up to 1,700 steps (requiring up to 34 chunk predictions), Fast-VLA achieved an 87.00% success rate, proving that fixed memory remains effective over long durations.

captions.F3: Rollout examples using fixed task memory. Across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO-10, and LIBERO-Plus with severe camera noise, tasks are successfully completed using solely the memory constructed at the start of each episode.
captions.F4: Attention transitions in a block-stacking task. As control transitions from the left arm to the right arm, head camera visual attention shifts from the red block to the green block, demonstrating that visual attention dynamically adapts to progress despite using fixed memory.

sections.heading: Conclusion: A Next-Generation VLA Design Decoupling Understanding from Control
sections.summary: By separating one-time task understanding from repetitive closed-loop control, Fast-VLA achieves massive speedups and memory savings. It demonstrates that the expressive power of large foundation models can be reconciled with real-time control responsiveness.
sections.details:
Fast-VLA takes a major step toward practical VLA deployment with a clear insight: "Understand the task once, and run only control in real time." Combining task memory generation via a 4B VLM at episode start with fast action prediction via a lightweight online actor, it cuts inference costs by an order of magnitude while maintaining success rates comparable to standard VLAs.

Comparative tests on identical hardware demonstrated a 10.9–17.1x inference speedup and a minimal 1.22 GiB resident memory footprint on RoboTwin 2.0. Memory swap experiments further verified that the actor genuinely relies on the context within the fixed memory. For robotics applications burdened by the computational weight of massive foundation models, this research provides a new architectural blueprint that maximizes performance while radically saving compute resources.

sections.heading: Appendix: Detailed Settings and Additional Robustness Verifications
sections.summary: Supplements details on hardware profiling protocols and additional qualitative rollout results under various environmental disturbances like viewpoint changes, lighting variations, and background textures.
sections.details:
### Inference Measurement Details
For a fair comparison of inference speeds, extensive profiling was conducted over 10,000 episodes (a total of 2,372,728 steps) on identical hardware. Out of Fast-VLA's 1.22 GiB online resident memory, the reused fixed task memory accounts for just 174.6 MiB.

### Additional Qualitative Rollout Verifications
Under various perturbations in LIBERO-Plus (camera viewpoint shifts, background pattern shifts, lighting changes, object placement shifts, and robot initial pose variations), Fast-VLA successfully completed drawer opening/closing and bowl placement tasks without breakdown, relying purely on the one-time task memory created from initial views.

captions.F6: Success cases under diverse environmental perturbations in LIBERO-Plus (camera positions, backgrounds, lighting, object layouts, initial poses). Even with fixed memory built from drastically altered initial views, it stably guides action generation throughout the episode.

takeaways: By separating the timescales of "task understanding" and "feedback control," massive VLMs can be moved out of the control loop to dramatically cut computational costs.
Preserving the Key–Value cache across all VLM layers as task memory allows the actor to flexibly extract visual and linguistic features at the right level of abstraction.
Dynamically injecting current wrist camera views and joint states into action queries enables flexible action generation suited to real-time progress, even when using fixed memory.
limitations: Because task memory is fixed at the start of an episode, adapting to dynamic tasks where human instructions change midway or the goal itself shifts remains untested.
Since the action decoder and head are trained from scratch on demonstration data, zero-shot generalization to completely unseen domains has its limits.
